full_judgment:
Mr. Md. Emdadul Haque Azad J:- This Rule, was issued at the instance of the defendant-respondent-petitioners calling upon the plaintiff appellant-opposite party Nos.1 and 2 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 08.02.2011 (decree signed on 14.02.2011) passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Rajbari in Title Appeal No.24 of 2007 allowing the appeal and reversing/setting aside the judgment and decree dated 29.01.2007 (decree signed on 05.02.2007) passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Rajbari Sardar, Rajbari in Title Suit No.55 of 2000 dismissing the suit should not be set aside. 

2. The fact relevant to the disposal of the instant Rule are that on 09.04.2000, the Opposite party Nos.1-2 as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No.55 of 2000 in the Court of the learned Assistant Judge, Sadar, Rajbari against the petitioners and the other opposite parties praying for a declaration that a registered kabuliyat being No.8264 dated 07.12.1999 executed in their name vide Settlement Case No. (XII-30/98-99)/(XII-151/95-96) for the period ranging from 29.09.1999 to 28.08.2000 is valid, effective and of legal force. 

3. The facts of the plaint of the aforesaid suit, in brief, are that the suit land belongs to the Government as khas land; that the plaintiffs took settlement of the same for 99 years from the Government vide Settlement Case No. (XII-30/98-99)/(XII-151/95-96) and as such a kabuliyat was registered in their name on 07.12.1999; that since settlement the plaintiffs have been enjoying and possessing the suit land by having the same mutated in their name and also by paying rent to the Government exchequer; that the plaintiffs have their homestead in the suit land and they have been possessing the same since the flood in 1988 by planting different trees; that they did not violate any of the terms of the kabuliyat dated 07.12.1999; that the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Rajbari Sader, Rajbari (defendant No.4) vide his letter dated 12.03.2000 asked the plaintiffs to appear before him for the purpose of hearing in respect of the Kabuliyat and that on his appearance the said defendant threatened to cancel their kabuliyat and hence, the suit. 

4. The Government as defendant Nos.1-4 contested the suit by filling a written statement denying the material facts of the plaint and contending, inter alia, that the suit land belongs to the Government as khas land and the same was settled/leased out in favour of the plaintiffs upon execution and registration of a bi-lateral deed of kabuliyat; that the suit land was also mutated in the name of the plaintiffs; that subsequently due to violation of the terms of the kabuliyat the Assistant Commissioner (Land) issued a notice upon the plaintiffs on 22.03.2000 and as such the said kabuliyat was cancelled later on; that the plaintiffs have no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land and therefore, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

5. The petitioner No.1 as added defendant No.6 contested the suit by filling a separate written statement denying the material facts of the plaint and contending, inter alia, that the suit land originally belonged to Satish Chandra Das, who granted settlement of the same along with other lands in favour of Mohammad Mozahar Ali Miah and Azhar Ali Miah; that in order to recover arrear k rents for 1360-1362 BS from the said tenants Azhar and Mozahar, Satish Chandra filed Rent Suit No.60 of 1957 in the Court of the then Munsif, Goalando and that suit was compromised between the parties on 26.02.1957; that while the said Azhar and 
Mozahar were enjoying and possessing the land, rent roll record was prepared in their name; that the said Mozahar Hossain transferred his share i.e. 181/2 decimals of land in favour of one Solemannesa by a registered sale deed dated 22.02.1961; that in order to sell the suit land Solemannesa entered into a contract for sale with the defendant-petitioner No.1 on 25.11.1988 fixing the consideration money at Tk.12,000/-; that following the death of Solemannesa her sons, Pran Sheikh and Ramzan Sheikh executed and registered a sale deed in his favour on 16.07.2000; that thereafter on 20.08.2000 the defendant-petitioner No.1 went to the local Tahshil Office to pay rent/land development tax and came to learn that the suit land has been recorded in the name of the Government instead of Solemannesa; that the Government has no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land; that the kabuliyat of the plaintiff's is collusive and ineffective; that the defendant-petitioner No.1 has right, title, interest and possession in the suit land and therefore, the suit is liable to be dismissed with cost. 

6. The predecessor of the petitioner Nos.2-6 as added defendant No.7 also contested the suit by filling another written statement denying the material facts of the plaint and contending, inter alia, that the suit land originally belonged to Satish Chandra Das, who granted settlement of the same along with other lands in favour of Azhar Ali Miah and Mozahar Ali Miah; that in order to recover arrear rents for 1360-1362 BS from the said tenants Azhar and Mozahar, Satish Chandra filed Rent Suit No.60 of 1957 in the Court of the then Munsif, Goalando and that suit was compromised between the parties on 26.02.1957; that pursuant to the said compromise decree, Azhar and Mozahar were admitted as tenants and they remained in possession of the suit land as owner thereof; that Azhar Miah died leaving behind widow Khodeja, 2 sons-Abdul Latif and Golam Sarwar and one daughter Jahanara Begum as his heirs; that the said heirs of Azhar Ali transferred the suit land in favour of the added defendant No.7 by a registered sale deed being No.4239 dated 15.06.1982 and delivered possession in his favour; that the suit land became uncultivable because of situation by the flood of 1988; that the ancestral/paternal residence of the plaintiff's was in Sujanagar, Pabna  and because of destruction of their house in Pabna by a flood in 1988, they stared looking for a piece of land for residential purposes; that the plaintiffs are the distant relatives of the said defendant No.7 and therefore, the latter allowed the former to live in the suit land on a temporary basis given the uncultivable nature of the suit land and accordingly, the plaintiffs erected homestead in the suit land in the first part of 1989 and started living therein and planted various trees; that at that time the plaintiffs undertook to vacate the suit land soon after they get another piece of suitable land; that in the middle of November, 2000 they claimed title to the suit land on the basis of a kabuliyat from the Government and that even being requested to vacate the suit land the plaintiffs refused to do so and as such the said defendant filed Title Suit No.214 of 2000 against the plaintiffs in the Court of the learned Assistant Judge, Rajbari Sader, Rajbari praying for a decree for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession; that the suit land is not at all the khas land of the Government and therefore, the suit is liable to be dismissed with cost. 

7. The suit was tried by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sader, Rajbari. During trail the plaintiffs examined 2 P.W.s and the defendant examined 6 D.W.s in support of their respective cases. 

8. The learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sader Rajbari by his judgment and decree dated 29.01.2006 (decree signed on 05.02.2006) dismissed the suit on contest holding that the suit is not maintainable and also that plaintiffs have no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land.

9. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid judgment and decree, the defendant-opposite party Nos.l-2 as appellants preferred Title Appeal No.24 of 2007 before the District Judge, Rajbari and the appeal was heard by the Joint District Judge, First Court, Rajbari, who by the judgment and decree dated 08.02.2011 (decree signed on 14.02.2011) allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment and decree passed by the trail court. 

10. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid judgment and decree dated 08.02.2011 passed by the Joint District Judge, First Court, Rajbari in Title Appeal No.24 of 2007, the petitioners moved an application under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and on 29.05.2011 obtained the present Rule and an interim order of stay. 

11. Mr. Zakir Hossain Bhuiyan, learned advocate appearing for the defendant-petitioners took me to the revisional-4 application, the impugned judgment and decree, the pleadings of the respective parties, the disposition of all the P.W.s and D.W.s and the documents exhibited by the parties and submits that the plaintiffs as well as the Government miserably failed to prove that the suit land vested in the Government as khas land during the S.A. operation in view of the fact that neither the plaintiffs nor the Government adducted any minimum iota of evidence including the khas khatian itself before the courts below in support of their contention nor did they disclose the source through which or the basis on which or the manner in which the suit land devolved upon the Government and as such the plea of khas khatian which is the genesis of the plaintiffs' claim falls flat and therefore, the suit is liable to be dismissed. In this connection Mr. Bhuiyan drew my attention to Section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and referred to the decision of Geeta Rani alias Shamima Khatun vs. Bangladesh, 36 DLR (AD) 225; Bangladesh and others vs. Mallick Ali Ahmed and others 3 CLR (AD) 345 and Md. Kalam Mollah and others vs. Sheikh Samsu and others, 23 BLT 320, which will be discussed later on.

12. Mr. Zakir Hossain Bhuiyan also submits that although the Government (defendant Nos.1-4) filed written statement and cross-examined the defendants' witnesses (DWs), they did not adduce any evidence of their own in support of their contention and as such their contention as raised in their written statement having not been supported/proved by any other evidence, oral or documentary, their written statement is liable to be discarded/kept out of consideration. In this regard Mr. Bhuiyan refers to the decisions of Md. Serajul Islam vs. Mrs. Hosne Ara Begum and others, 34 BLD 55; Asgar Ali Mia and others vs. Bangladesh and others, 16 BLC 37 and Sreejukta Haladhar Karmakar and others vs. Bangladesh and others, 16 BLD 519. 

13. Mr. Zakir Hossain Bhuiyan further submits that the plaintiffs as well as the defendant Nos.1-4 (the Government) did not neither specifically deny the accuracy or genuineness of R.S. Khatian No.259 (Exhibit-1/Ka of Title Suit No.214 of 2000) nor did they take any step against the said R.S. Khatian prepared and published in the name of Satish Chandra Das and as such the same has got presumptive value of correction in view of the case of Government of Bangladesh and others vs. Mrs. Mohsina Rahaman alias Joya as reported in 50 DLR 186, wherein it has been held that : 
"The settled law is that R.S. record has a presumption of correctness but the S.A. record has no such presumptive value" 

14. Drawing my attention to paragraph 3 of the plaint, Mr. Bhuiyan submits that the plaintiffs were inducted as tenant at will into 18.50 decimals of land belonging to the defendant No.7 on the prayer of the former that they lost their homestead in Sujangar, Pabna by the devastating flood of 1988, which is otherwise admitted by the plaintiffs in paragraph 3 of the plaint. The relevant portion of the said paragraph of the plaint is reproduced below:

“-------ইং ১৯৮৮ সালের বন্যার করাল গ্রাসে বাদীর চরের বাড়ী বিনষ্ট হইলে নালিশী দাবীকৃত ভূমি পতিত জমি হিসাবে বাদী উক্ত জমিতে ঘরবাড়ী উত্তোলন ও গাছপালা লাগাইয়া ভোগ দখলকার হয়েন ও খাকেন।”

On the above point as to the plaintiffs entry into the half portion of the suit land Mr. Bhuiyan submits that form the above-quoted averments made in paragraph 3 of the plaint it is abundantly clear that had the suit land even been vested in the Government as khas land, the same would have been leased out by the Government in favour of any other person/s and in the absence of any such lease it inevitable suggests that the suit land never devolved upon the Government. In this connection Mr. Bhuiyan further submits that the plaintiffs' entered into the suit land in 1988 finding the same as vacant land is nothing but cock and bull story in view of the fact that had the suit land been actually vacant the local people would have taken possession thereof much earlier leaving no room for a stranger coming from a different district called Pabna to occupy the same and erect homestead thereon. 

15. Mr. Bhuiyan next submits that the defendant-petitioners have lawful right, title, interest and possession in the suit land on the strength of their and their predecessors registered sale deeds dated 22.02.1961 (Exhibit-1 of Title Suit No.154 of 2000), sale deed dated 15.06.1982 (Exhibit-5 of Title Suit No.214 of 2000) and sale deed dated 16.07.2000 (Exhibit-3 of Title Suit No.214 of 2000) and those registered sale deeds being documents of title, will prevail over the so-called and non-existent S.A. khatian mysteriously prepared in the name of the Government. In this connection Mr. Bhuiyan placed reliance on 18 BLC (AD) 44; 13 MLR (AD) 6; 32 (DLR) 252; 5 MLR 374. In the case of Abdul Mannan Bhuiyan and others vs. Md. Nasir Hossain and others, 18 BLC (AD) 44, our Appellate Division unanimously held that: 

"Registered document prevail upon record of right-SA and RS records were not an evidence of title and that a registered document would prevail upon the records of rights and that the registered document would remain in force unless the same was cancelled by an appropriate civil court." 

16. On the question of burden of proof, Mr. Bhuiyan submits that the plaintiffs ought to have proved their case on the balance of probabilities without capitalizing on the weakness, if any, of the defendant-petitioners, but the Court of appeal below most illegally and in clear violation of the provisions of the Evidence Act, 1872 shifted the plaintiffs' burden of proof on the defendant-petitioners and as such the impugned judgment and decree being based on grossly perverse findings, is illegal and liable to be set aside. As to the point of the plaintiff's burden of proof, Mr. Bhuiyan referred to the decision reported in 58 DLR; I ADC 401; 8 MLR (AD) 41; 48 DLR 208; 39 DLR (AD) 237 and 9 BLT (AD) 66. 

17. Mr. Bhuiyan goes on to submit that the lower appellate Court committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure justice in failing to appreciate that Plot No.185 was present/included in R.S. Khatian No.259 and as such the observation that the said plot is missing in the khatian is patently perverse and totally contrary to the record of the case. 
Taking me to paragraph 7 .of the plaint, Mr. Bhuiyan submits that the suit of the plaintiffs is premature in view of the fact that their so-called kabuliyat was not cancelled, rather the same was merely threatened to be cancelled and such threat of cancellation as opposed to any final decision actually canceling the lease is not a cause of action and therefore, the suit being based on a mere apprehension, is without any cause of action and liable to be dismissed. In this regard, Mr. Bhuiyan placed reliance on paragraph 7 of the plaint is reproduced below:
“৭। সহকারী কমিশনার (ভীমি) রাজবাড়ী সদর নালিশী দাবীকৃত ভূমি সংক্রান্ত ইং ১২-৩-২০০০ তাং স্বাক্ষরিত নোটিশ বাদ প্রাপ্ত হইয়া ইং ৩-৪-২০০০ তাং সহকারী কমিশনার (ভূমি) রাজবাড়ী সদর নালিশী দাবীকৃত ভূমি সংক্রান্ত কবুলিয়ত বাতিলের জন্য হুমকি প্রদর্শন করায় অত্র নালিশের কারন উদ্ভব হইয়াছে।”

18. Mr. Bhuiyan continues to submit that the lower appellate Court failed to appreciate that the weight of evidence and preponderance of documents was totally in favour of the defendant-petitioners and against the opposite parties and that the petitioners have been able to prove their lawful right, title, interest and possession in the suit land by both documentary and oral evidence through competent witnesses of convincing nature and as such Court of appeal below ought to have dismissed the appeal and upheld the judgment and decree passed by the learned trail Court. 

19. Mr. Bhuiyan lastly submits that the learned trail Court correctly dismissed the suit on merit upon proper assessment of the pleadings, evidence and other materials on record, but the learned Court of appeal below misread and mis-appreciated the evidence and materials on record and came to an erroneous decision since as the final Court of fact it did not apply its judicial mind and independently asses the evidence and other materials on record in violation of its mandatory obligation under Order 41 Rule 31 and 33 of the: Code of Civil Procedure, rather turned down the decision of the learned trial Court on some perverse, unfounded and untenable findings without assigning any reason and also without reversing the findings of the learned trail Court and as such the impugned judgment and decree being not a proper judgment of reversal, is illegal and liable to be set aside, and in support of his submission Mr. Bhuiyan has placed reliance on the decision reported in XII ADC 751; 14 BLD 229; 17 BLD 47; 10 MLR 255; 15 BLD 96. 

20. On the other hand, Mr. Shah Hossain, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite party Nos.1-2 submits that on and from 14` April, 1956 the rent receiving interest of all the rent receivers in Bangladesh having been acquired by the Government under Section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (the SAT Act), the defendant-petitioners' claim of title to the suit land on the strength of a compromise decree dated 26.02.1957 drawn up in Rent Suit No.60 of 1957 between the then Zamindar/landlord Satish Chandra Das and his tenants Mohammad Mozahar Ali Miah and Azhar Ali Miah from whom the petitioners got the suit land by way of successive transfers becomes barred by law. In support of his submission, Mr. Hossain referred to the decisions reported in 31 DLR (AD) 323; 14 BLC 848; 38 DLR (AD) 93 and 20 DLR 699. Amongst the cited decisions, I feel the necessity to quote the ratio decidendi of the case of Government of Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Mymensing vs. Abani Kanta Chakraborty and others 38 DLR (AD) 93, which runs as follows : 

"After the abolition of all rent receiving interests in the country there is only one class of tenancy under the Government whose rights and liabilities are governed by an uniform law." 

21. Controverting the above submission readily, Mr. Bhuiyan submits that Rent Suit No.60 of 1957 was filed by the then Zaminder Satish Chandra Das for realizing the arrear rent in respect of the suit land for 1360-1362 BS (corresponding to 1953-1955) and the said Rent Suit having been field within 3 (three) years for realizing the arrear rents for the period before Section 3 of the SAT Act came into force, the said Rent Suit is maintainable within the meaning of Article 110 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1908 and therefore, the compromise decree drawn up in that suit is legal, whereby the landlord Satish Chandra Das admitted Mozahar Ali and Azhar Ali as his tenants for the period prior to Section 3 of the SAT Act came into force and following the acquisition of the rent receiving interest by the Government, the said tenants Mozahar Ali and Azahar Ali became direct tenants under the Government and the petitioners having acquired title to the suit land by successive transfers by dint of 3(three) separate registered sale deeds of 1961, 1982 and 2000 from them and their transferees, are the lawful title holders of the suit land. 

22. Mr. Shah Hossain also submits that the defendant-petitioners produced and exhibited the certified copies of their title deed in support of their defence/claim to the suit land without any formal proof thereof and as such those secondary evidences in support of their title are not admissible in law within the meaning of Section 63 and 65 of the Evidence Act, 1872. To substantiate his submission, Mr. Hossain cited the decisions reported in 47 DLR (AD) 45; 41 DLR (AD) 97 and 14 BLC (AD) 132. In the case of Soya Rani Guha alias Soya Rani Gupta vs. Abdul Awal Miah and others 47 DLR (AD) 45, it has been held that : 

"A party producing secondary evidence of a document is not relieved of the duty of proving the execution of the original. Even where a document is exhibited without objection the Court is to be satisfied as to its execution." 

23. In reply to the above submission, Mr. Zakir Hossain Bhuiyan submits that the certified copy of the title deeds of the defendant-petitioners are admissible in law within the meaning of Section 79 of the Evidence Act, 1872 in view of the fact that as registered documents those sale deeds carry the presumption of correctness of the endorsement made therein and if the opposite parties intend to dispute that presumption they are required to dislodge the correctness of the endorsement (Shishir Kanti Pal and others vs. Nur Mohammad and others, 55 DLR (AD) 39). In this connection Mr. Bhuiyan further submits that the decision reported in 55 DLR (AD) 39 being later in point of time will prevail over the one reported in 47 DLR (AD) 45. 

24. Mr. Shah Hossain next submits that the S.A. Khatian prepared and published in the name of the Government vis-à-vis the suit land shall be presumed to be correct unless and until it is proved by evidence to be incorrect. In this connection Mr. Hossain referred to Section 19(3) and 144A of the SAT Act and the decisions reported in 9 MLR (AD) 82; 30 DLR (SC) 81; 6 BLC 241; 33 DLR 126; 17 BLC (AD) 174 and 61 DLR 18. 

Mr. Shah Hossain finally submits that the learned trial Court wrongly shifted the burden of proving the correctness of S.A. Khatian on the plaintiff-opposite parties, and the appellate Court below as the final Court of fact arrived at a proper decision upon proper assessment of the pleadings of the parties, evidence and other materials on ' record and as such the same does not call for any interference from this Court. 

25. I have meticulously gone through the revisional application, the impugned judgment and decree, the pleadings of the respective parties, evidence led by them and other materials on record and also heard the learned Advocates for both the sides at length and perused the decisions relied upon by both the parties with utmost circumspection and the relevant provisions of law wherefrom it transpires that the preparation and publication of S.A. record of rights, if any, in the khas khatians of the Government as well as the maintainability of Rent Suit No.60 of 1957 are the predominant issues in this case apart from other connected issues and I will endeavor to address all the issues in proportion to their respective weight and importance. 

26. It is the case of the plaintiff-opposite party Nos.1-2 and the Government (defendant Nos.1-4) that the suit land vested in the Government as khas land during the S.A. operation, but neither the plaintiffs nor the Government adduced any evidence including the khas khatian itself before the Courts below in support of their contention. Again, although the Government filed a written statement, they did not adduce any evidence, oral or documentary, to show as to when, why and how the suit land became khas in their name and as such the written statement of the Government will not ipso facto be admissible in evidence unless and until the same is supported by competent witness of convincing nature, and as such Section 92 of the SAT Act as well as the decisions referred to by the defendant: petitioners will stand in the way of the claim of plaintiff-opposite party Nos.1-2 as well as the Government. At this juncture I think it is necessary to quote Section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, which runs as follow: 
"92(1) The interest of a raiyat in a holding shall be extinguished —
(a) when he dies intestate leaving no heir entitled to inherit under the law of inheritance to which he is subject; 
(b) when he surrenders his holding at the end of any agricultural year by giving notice in the prescribed form and in the prescribed manner and within the prescribed period to the Revenue-officer; 
(c) when he voluntarily abandons his residence without making any arrangement for payment of the rent as it falls due and cesses to cultivate his holding either by himself or by members of his family or by, or with the aid of, servants or laborers or with the aid of, partners or bargadars for a period of three successive years; Or - 
(d) when such interest has devolved by inheritance, under the law of inheritance to which such raiyat is subject, on a person who is not a bona fide cultivator and such person has not cultivated the land comprised in the holding either by himself or by members of his family or by, or with the aid of, servants or laborers or with the aid of, partners or bargadars during the period of five years from the date on which such interest has so devolved on him and there is no sufficient cause why he has not so cultivated the land. 

(2) When the interest of a raiyat in a holding is extinguished under sub-section (1), the Revenue-officer may enter on the holding; and the holding shall, with effect from the date on which the Revenue-officer so enters on it, vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances except the encumbrances on the holding which is extinguished under clause (a) of the said sub-section, but the persons whose interests in the holdings are extinguished under clauses (b), (c) and (d) of that sub-section shall continue to be personally liable for the money secured by the encumbrances on such holdings. 
(3) Before entering on a holding under sub-section (2), the Revenue-officer shall cause a notice to be published in the prescribed manner declaring his intention to so enter on the holding and specifying the reasons thereof and also inviting objections from all persons interested in the holding and shall consider any objections that may be submitted to him within the period specified in that behalf in the notice and shall record a decision.

(5)----------------   

27. In the case of Bangladesh and others vs. Mallick Ali Ahmed and others, 3 CLR (AD) 345, it has been held: 
"The treating of the suit land as escheat property by the government and thereby declaring the same as khas land of the government without making it clear in any manner as to how and why the suit property can be treated as escheat property has been illegal." 
It is pertinent to mention here that the Government did not turn up before the Courts below as well as this Court in the course of the Rule hearing to establish its claim to the suit land and therefore, the plaintiffs as well as the Government signally failed to prove that the suit land ever vested in the Government as khas land in view of the Government's failure to adduce evidence in support of its written statement. This view finds support from the case of Md. Serajul Islam vs. Mrs, Hosne Ara Begum and others 34 BLD 55, wherein it has been held that: 

"The filing of the written statement without giving any oral testimony in support of the same before the Court below and without facing cross-examination the same will not be considered ipso facto as evidence, rather, either of the pleadings must be proved by giving oral evidence." 

28. It appears from Ext.2 of Title Suit No.214 of 2000 (from which Civil Revision No.2748 of 2014 arose and which has been heard and disposed of in simultaneous with the present Rule) that Rent Suit No.60 of 1957 was filed by the then Zaminder Satish Chandra Das against his tenants Mozahar Ali Miah and Azahar Ali Miah for realizing the arrear rent in respect of the suit land for 1360-1362 BS (corresponding to 1953-1955) and the said Rent Suit was filed within 3(three) years for realizing the arrear rents for the period prior to Section 3 of the SAT Act came into force as on 14th April, 1956 and hence, the said Rent Suit is maintainable within the meaning of Article 110 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1908 and therefore, the compromise decree dated 26.02.1957 (Ext.2 of Title Suit No. 214 of 2000) drawn up in that rent suit is also legal. In this connection I think it would be profitable to quote Article 110 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1908, which runs as follows: 
Description of suit	Period of limitation	Time from which period begins to run
110. For arrears of rent.	Part VI-Three years (cntd) Three years	When the arrears become due


It also appears from the abovementioned compromise decree dated 26.02.1957 that landlord Satish Chandra Das admitted Mozahar Ali and Azahar Ali as his tenants for the period prior to Section 3 of the SAT Act came into force and following the acquisition of the rent receiving interest by the Government, the said tenants Mozahar Ali and Azahar Ali became direct tenants under the Government and the petitioners having acquired their title to the suit land by successive transfers by dint of 3(three) separate registered sale deeds dated 01.03.1961 (Ext.2 of Title Suit No.154 of 2000), 15.06.1982 (Ext.5 of Title Suit No.214 of 2000) and 16.07.2000 (Ext.3 of Title Suit No.154 of 2000) from them and their transferees, are the lawful title holders of the suit land. 

29. It is a settled principle of law that the plaintiff has to prove his case on the balance of probabilities and he/she cannot bank or capitalize on the weakness of the defendant. But the Court of appeal below turned down this century-old settled proposition and wrongly shifted the plaintiffs' burden of proof on the defendants by holding that "---কিন্তু নথি পর্যালোচন দেখা যায়  যে বিজ্ঞ নিম্ন আদালত সাক্ষ্য আইনের প্রচলিত বিধি লংঘন করে ৬-৭নং পক্ষভূক্ত বিবাদীর Barden of Proof বাদী ও ১-৪ নং বিবাদীর উপর ন্যস্ত করেছেন। ৬-৭নং পক্ষভূ্ক্ত বিবাদী তাদের জবাবে নালিশী জমিতে স্বত্বের দাবীর সর্মথনে যে সব দলিলপত্র দাখিল করেছেন তা পর্যালোচনা দেখা যায় যে আর এস ২৫৯ খতিয়ারেন ১৮৫ দাগের জমি উল্লেখ নাই। আর এস ২৫৯ খতিয়ানে ১৮৫ দাগই নাই। অথচ বিজ্ঞ নিম্ন আদালত ৬-৭ নং বিবাদীর কাগজপত্র সঠিকভাবে পর্যালোচনা ও অনুধোবন না করেই ৬-৭ বিবাদীর কাগজপত্র বিশ্বাস করেছে। এস এ খতিয়ান কিভাবে সরকারের নামে হয়েছে বিজ্ঞ নিম্ন আদালত তা প্রমানের ভার বাদী ও ১-৪ নং বিবাদী সরকারের উপর অর্পন করে গুরুতর ভূল সিদ্ধান্তে উপনীত হয়েছেন কেননা Record of Rights এ অবশ্যই একটি Legal Presumption আছে।-----------

30. The above findings of the lower appellate Court is erroneous and perverse on two counts, firstly since the plaintiff-opposite party Nos.1-2 and the Government claim the suit land to be the khas land of the Government, it is their bounden duty of proof their contention: There exists a large body of case law on this point. For instance, in the case of Md. Naimuddin Sarder @ Naimuddin Sarder vs. Md. Abdul Kalam Biswas @ Md. Abul Kalam Basiruddin @ Abul Kalam Azad and another, 39 DLR (AD) 237, it has been held that: 

"Plaintiff in order to succeed must establish his own case to obtain a decree and weakness of the defendant's case is no ground for passing a decree in favour of the plaintiff." 

Secondly, it is as clear as broad daylight from R.S. Khatian No.259 (Ext.l of Title Suit No.154 of 2000) that R.S. Plot No.185 is present in the .said khatian showing 37 decimals of land in sixteen annas share. On this point the learned Advocate for the opposite party Nos.1-2 submits that the said finding is merely a slip of pen on the part of the lower appellate Court and in fact the appellate Court below meant R.S. Khatian No.148 (Ext. 1/Ka of Title Suit No.154 of 2000). On scrutiny of R.S. Khatian No.148, it is found that Plot No.285 appears therein, but the quantum of land in the said plot is completely different, namely 15 decimals in eight annas share. Moreover, lands of both the R.S. Khatian being Nos.259 and 148 belonged to Zaminder Satish Chandra Das and as such I find it difficult to accept the submissions advanced from the plaintiffs on this point. Rather, I subscribe to the view that the Court of appeal below wrongly recorded the said finding as to R.S. Khatian No.259 and Plot No.185 upon his total non-application of judicial mind to the materials on record, which is very unbecoming and deplorable on the part of a judicial officer. 

31. It appears from paragraph 3 of the plaint that the plaintiffs entered into the suit land after the flood of 1988 whereas they allegedly took settlement of the same in 1999 and they did not at all clarify in their pleadings submitted and evidences adduced in any of the suits in what capacity they possessed and enjoyed the suit land for the intervening period between 1988 and 1999 and as such I am constrained to hold the view that the plaintiffs entered into the suit land as -mere trespassers. Moreover, I think that if the suit land had ever been recorded in the khas khatian of the Government, it would have settled the same in favour of anyone one else, and in the absence of any such lease, government's title to the suit land is not proved at all and therefore, the claim of the plaintiffs also fails since they are claiming interest in the suit land through the Government. 

Furthermore, the plaintiffs stated in paragraph 7 of the plaint that the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Rajbari Sadar, Rajbari (defendant No.4 to the suit) by his letter dated 12.03.2000 merely threatened to cancel their kabuliyat, but at no point of time their lease was actually cancelled, and the threat of cancellation as opposed to any actual cancellation is merely an apprehension which cannot substitute the cause of action of the suit as framed and therefore, the suit is premature and liable to be dismissed as being not maintainable in law as per the decision given in the case of Kamaluddin (Md.) and another vs. Secretary, Ministry of Land, Bangladesh and others 56 DLR (AD) 212, wherein it has been held that: 
"unless final order is passed in a matter, person interested in the matter or persons apprehensive of being affected by the act of the functionaries -- performing functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority is not entitled to invoke the writ jurisdiction." 

It is worth to mention here that although the above decision has been made on a writ petition, the same extends to civil jurisdiction as well given the fact that writ jurisdiction forms part of civil jurisdiction. 

32. As I have already found that the plaintiffs are mere trespassers into the suit land, they have neither got any locus standi to institute the present suit nor to question the accuracy or genuineness of the title deeds of the defendant-petitioners, however, defective title the letters might have to the suit land. On the 'balance of probabilities' which is the standard of proof in civil jurisdiction as opposed to 'beyond reasonable doubt' in criminal jurisdiction and also on the weight of evidence and preponderance of documents available in the records of the case, it appears to me that the defendant-petitioners have lawful title to the suit land, which can be questioned only by a person having a better title thereto. That not being so, the case of the plaintiffs totally fails. 

33. On perusal of the pleadings, evidence and other materials on record, I am of the considered view that the judgment of the trial Court is very much sound, proper and in accordance with law for the reasons stated above and it does not suffer from any Misreading or non-reading of evidence or non-consideration or misconstruction of any document affecting the merit of the case and as such I find no reason to interfere with the same. On the other hand, the Court of appeal below misread and mis-appreciated the provisions of law, the evidence and materials on record and came to an erroneous decision by failing to apply its judicial mind to the given set of facts and as such it failed to independently assesses the evidence and other materials on record in violation of its mandatory obligation under Order 41 Rule 31 and 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure since it turned down the decision of the trial Court on some perverse, unfounded and untenable findings without assigning any reason and also without reversing the findings of the trial Court and thus, the impugned judgment and decree being not a proper judgment of reversal, is illegal and liable to be set aside. 

34. Accordingly, I find merit in the Rule for which it succeeds. In the result, the Rule is made absolute and the judgment and decree dated 08.02.2011 (decree signed on 14.02.2011) passed by the Joint District Judge, First Court, Rajbari in Title Appeal No.24 of 2007 allowing the appeal is hereby set aside and the judgment and decree dated 29.01.2007 (decree signed on 05.02.2007) passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Rajbari Sadar, Rajbari in Title Suit No.55 of 2000 dismissing the suit is hereby affirmed. 

35. No order as to cost. The interim order of stay granted earlier at the time of issuance of the Rule is hereby vacated. 

36. Send down the Lower Court Record along with a copy of this judgment to the Court concerned at once. 

End.
